content:
The Quran, the critic says, was "borrowed" from the rabbis. Abraham Geiger argued it in 1833, and W. St. Clair Tisdall repeated it for a missionary readership in The Original Sources of the Qur'an (1905).[1]

This article aims to provide context to that claim, insha'Allah, on a single subject: Jesus. We set five passages of the Babylonian Talmud beside what the Quran says of the same man and his mother.

"They rejected Faith; that they uttered against Mary a grave false charge" (4:156). The Quran names the slander and condemns it.[2]

Tractate Sanhedrin 43a reports that "Yeshu" was hanged on the eve of Passover, after a herald had announced for forty days that he would be stoned for sorcery and for leading Israel astray.[3]

Peter Schäfer of Princeton reads these stories as a deliberate "counter-Gospel": the rabbis knew the Gospel narrative and answered it, maintaining that Jesus was rightly executed as a blasphemer and idolater.[4]

The Quran answers the boast itself: "they killed him not, nor crucified him, but so it was made to appear to them" (4:157). The Talmud claims the execution. The Quran denies it.

Tractate Shabbat 104b names a "ben Stada" and explains that his mother's husband was Stada while the man who fathered him was Pandeira. The Gemara adds that his mother was Miriam and that "Stada" was a nickname for her straying.[5]

The Gospel of John already shows the taunt in embryo. His opponents tell Jesus, "We were not born of sexual immorality" (John 8:41, ESV).

The Quran defends Mary at every turn. It calls the charge against her a "grave false charge" (4:156), records her people's accusation only to have the infant answer it (19:27 to 33), and says God chose her above the women of all nations (3:42).

Strength: firm. On the honour of Mary the two texts stand at opposite poles.

Sanhedrin 107b tells of "Yeshu the Nazarene", a pupil of Yehoshua ben Perachiah, and gives the verdict that he "practised magic and deceived and led Israel astray".[6]

The charge is older than the Talmud. The Pharisees said he cast out demons "by Beelzebul, the prince of demons" (Matthew 12:24, ESV), and after the crucifixion they called him "that impostor" (Matthew 27:63, ESV).

The Quran gives the same works their true source. Jesus healed the blind and the leper and raised the dead "by My leave", God says, and it was the disbelievers who called it "nothing but evident magic" (5:110).

Strength: firm. The Quran repeats the accusation in order to reject it.

Gittin 56b to 57a tells how Onkelos, a nephew of the emperor Titus, raised the dead by necromancy before converting to Judaism. He asks "Yeshu" his punishment in the next world, and is told: "He is punished with boiling excrement."[7]

The Quran says the opposite of the same man's place in the next world: he is "held in honour in this world and the Hereafter and of (the company of) those nearest to Allah" (3:45).

Muslims are not asked to share any of this. We report it because the critic claims the Quran was taken from these books.

Not every reader accepts that "Yeshu" means Jesus of Nazareth. The medieval authority Asher ben Jehiel held that the Yeshu of the Talmud is a different man, and the Jewish Virtual Library judges the Ben Stada tradition "highly unlikely" to reach back to the tannaitic period.[8]

Schäfer holds the other view, that the Babylonian rabbis knew the Gospels, especially Matthew and John, and wrote these stories against them.[9] Either way the result is the same for the critic.

If the passages concern Jesus, the Quran contradicts its supposed teachers on the man it calls the Messiah. If they concern someone else, the rabbis had nothing on Jesus for the Quran to take. We set out the other "borrowing" claims in Talmud, midrash and apocrypha: 6 answers on borrowing claims.

The bottom line

Five passages, and the Quran contradicts every one. The Talmud boasts of his execution, slanders his mother, calls his miracles sorcery and sets him in boiling excrement. The Quran denies the crucifixion, clears Mary, credits the miracles to God and places Jesus among those nearest to Him.

A book that reverses its supposed source on the central question was not copied from it. "Say: He is Allah, the One and Only" (112:1), and His messenger Jesus is defended in His book. Allah knows best.

Notes

  1. Abraham Geiger, Was hat Mohammed aus dem Judenthume aufgenommen? (Bonn, 1833); W. St. Clair Tisdall, The Original Sources of the Qur'an (London: SPCK, 1905).
  2. Quran 4:156, A. Yusuf Ali translation.
  3. Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 43a. Peter Schäfer, Jesus in the Talmud (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2007), discusses the passage in his chapter on the execution.
  4. Schäfer, Jesus in the Talmud, as summarised by Princeton University Press and by its reviewers in Studies in Christian-Jewish Relations.
  5. Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 104b, with the parallel in Sanhedrin 67a. The Jewish Virtual Library entry "Ben Stada" records that both traditions were cut in part from later editions by Christian censorship.
  6. Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 107b; the same verdict stands in Sanhedrin 43a.
  7. Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 57a, William Davidson translation on Sefaria, which glosses "that man" as a euphemism for Jesus. The Talmud gives the reason elsewhere: one who mocks the words of the Sages is sentenced to boiling excrement.
  8. Jewish Virtual Library, "Ben Stada"; Wikipedia, "Yeshu", for Asher ben Jehiel.
  9. Schäfer, Jesus in the Talmud.
